A characterization of positive spanning sets with ties to
strongly edge-connected digraphs

August 24, 2026
Abstract

Positive spanning sets (PSSs) are families of vectors that span a given linear space through non-negative linear combinations. Despite certain classes of PSSs being well understood, a complete characterization of PSSs remains elusive. In this paper, we explore a relatively understudied relationship between positive spanning sets and strongly edge-connected digraphs, in that the former can be viewed as a generalization of the latter. We leverage this connection to define a decomposition structure for positive spanning sets inspired by the ear decomposition from digraph theory.

Keywords

Positive spanning sets; Positive bases; Strongly edge-connected digraphs;
Ear decomposition; Network matrices; Gaussian elimination.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification

05C20; 05C50; 15A21; 15B99.

1 Introduction

Gaussian elimination is a fundamental technique in linear algebra, that can be used to assess whether a given matrix is linearly spanning, in the sense that its columns span the entire space through linear combinations [17, Page 6]. Similarly, in graph theory, one can determine a spanning tree of a graph using linear algebra techniques, while efficient implementations of graph algorithms can be obtained by leveraging sparse linear algebra [10].

Positive spanning sets, or PSSs, are matrices such that the columns span the entire space through nonnegative linear combinations [7]. These matrices are instrumental to direct-search algorithms, a class of continuous optimization algorithms that proceed by exploring the variable space through suitably chosen directions [16, 2]. When those directions are chosen from positive spanning sets, convergence can be guaranteed at a rate that heavily depends on the properties of the PSSs at hand [16, 9]. In this setting, using a direction corresponds to evaluating an expensive function, and thus optimizers typically rely on inclusion-wise minimal positive spanning sets, or positive bases [21, 22]. Although positive bases have already been fully described [24], generic descriptions are often impractical to generate positive bases in practice. As a result, optimizers have focused on characterizing special positive bases for which simpler characterizations can be obtained [13, 14].

Perhaps surprisingly, a connection between positive spanning sets and strongly edge-connected digraphs was spotted early in the PSS literature [19], but to the authors’ knowledge this connection has not been exploited further. Meanwhile, numerous results have been established for strongly connected digraphs [3, 15], with minimal strongly edge-connected digraphs attracting recent interest [1, 6, 11, 12]. Although such digraphs appear connected to positive bases through the concept of minimality, a formal link between those objects has yet to be described.

In this paper, we provide certificates for the positive spanning property based on digraph theory. To this end, we show that PSSs can be seen as generalizing the concept of strongly edge-connected digraphs. We then leverage this connection to obtain a novel characterization of such matrices based on the ear decomposition of digraphs [25].

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review key results from digraph theory. We then discuss positive spanning sets and draw connections with strongly edge-connected digraphs in Section 3. Our main results, that generalize the ear decomposition to positive spanning sets, are derived in Section 4.

Notations

Throughout this paper, we work in the Euclidean space ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with n≥2n\geq 2, or a linear subspace thereof, denoted by 𝕃⊂ℝn\mathbb{L}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}. The dimension of such a subspace will always be assumed to be at least 11. The set of real matrices with nn rows and mm columns will be denoted as ℝn×m\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}. Those dimensions will always be assumed to be at least 11. Bold lowercase letters (e.g. 𝐯\mathbf{v},𝐚\mathbf{a}) will be used to designate vectors and arcs in directed graphs, while bold uppercase letters (e.g. 𝐃\mathbf{D}) will denote matrices. The notations 𝟎n\mathbf{0}_{n} and 𝟏n\mathbf{1}_{n} will respectively be used to designate the null vector and the all-ones vector in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, while 𝐈𝐧=[𝐞𝟏…𝐞𝐧]\mathbf{I_{n}}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{e_{1}}&\dots&\mathbf{e_{n}}\end{bmatrix} will denote the identity matrix in ℝn×n\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}. Given a matrix 𝐃∈ℝn×m\mathbf{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}, its set of columns will be denoted col⁡(𝐃)\cols(\mathbf{D}) while its linear span (i.e.i.e. the set of linear combinations of its columns) will be denoted by span⁡(𝐃)\spann(\mathbf{D}). The matrix whose entries are the signs of those of 𝐌\mathbf{M} will be noted s​g​n​(𝐌)sgn(\mathbf{M}). Calligraphic letters such as 𝒟\mathcal{D} and 𝒮\mathcal{S} will be used for finite families of vectors or of indices. For any integer m≥1m\geq 1, we let [[1,m]]:={z:1≤z≤m,z∈ℤ}[\![1,m]\!]:=\{z:1\leq z\leq m,z\in\mathbb{Z}\}. Finally, for a digraph G=(V,A)G=(V,A) the notations (u,v)(u,v) and u−vu-v will respectively designate an arc and an oriented path in AA going from uu to vv.

2 Digraphs and ear decomposition

In this section, we recall classical results on the ear decomposition for digraphs. For sake of completeness, we first define the main concepts and properties of digraphs to be used throughout the paper [3, 25]. We consider digraphs of the form G=(V,A)G=(V,A), where VV denotes a set of vertices and AA denotes a set of arcs. A directed path in GG is a sequence of arcs of the form {(ui,ui+1)}i=1,…,k\{(u_{i},u_{i+1})\}_{i=1,\dots,k}. Directed paths such that u1=uk+1u_{1}=u_{k+1} with u2,…,uku_{2},\dots,u_{k} all distinct are called circuits. A digraph (V,A)(V,A) is called acyclic if the set AA does not contain any circuit, while it is called strongly edge-connected - or strongly connected for simplicity- if for any (u,v)∈V2(u,v)\in V^{2}, there exists a directed path from uu to vv. A strongly connected digraph G=(V,A)G=(V,A) is minimally strongly connected if any digraph G′=(V,A′)G^{\prime}=(V,A^{\prime}) such that A′⊂AA^{\prime}\subset A, |A′|=|A|−1|A^{\prime}|=|A|-1 is not strongly connected. Finally, an oriented spanning tree of a graph GG is an oriented tree T=(V,A^)T=(V,\hat{A}) such that A^⊂A\hat{A}\subset A.

As mentioned in the previous section, we are interested in certifying whether a digraph is strongly connected. Proposition 2.1 provides a negative certificate for this property.

Proposition 2.1

A connected digraph G=(V,A)G=(V,A) is not strongly edge-connected if and only if there exists an oriented cut of GG, i.e. a set A~⊂A\tilde{A}\subset A and two vertex-disjoint subgraphs G1=(V1,A1)G_{1}=(V_{1},A_{1}) and G2=(V2,A2)G_{2}=(V_{2},A_{2}) of GG with V1≠∅V_{1}\neq\emptyset, V2≠∅V_{2}\neq\emptyset, such that

A=A~∪A1∪A2and∀(u,v)∈A~,u∈V1​and​v∈V2.A=\tilde{A}\cup A_{1}\cup A_{2}\quad\text{and}\quad\forall(u,v)\in\tilde{A},\quad u\in V_{1}\ \mbox{and}\ v\in V_{2}.

Proof. Suppose first that there exists an oriented cut of GG given by A~⊂A\tilde{A}\subset A, G1=(V1,A1)G_{1}=(V_{1},A_{1}) and G2=(V2,A2)G_{2}=(V_{2},A_{2}). Let v1∈V1v_{1}\in V_{1} and v2∈V2v_{2}\in V_{2}. By definition of an oriented cut, there does not exist a directed path in AA joining v2v_{2} to v1v_{1}, proving that GG is not strongly connected.

Conversely, suppose that GG is not strongly connected and let v1,v2v_{1},v_{2} be two vertices for which there is no v2−v1v_{2}-v_{1} path in AA. Let V2⊂VV_{2}\subset V be the set of vertices vv such that AA contains a v2−vv_{2}-v path and let V1=V∖V2V_{1}=V\setminus V_{2}. If A1A_{1} (resp. A2A_{2}) denotes the set of arcs between vertices of V1V_{1} (resp. V2V_{2}), then G1=(V1,A1)G_{1}=(V_{1},A_{1}), G2=(V2,A2)G_{2}=(V_{2},A_{2}) and A~=A\(A1∪A2)\tilde{A}=A\backslash\left(A_{1}\cup A_{2}\right) define an oriented cut for GG as by construction, the arcs in A~\tilde{A} must be of the form (u1,u2)(u_{1},u_{2}) with u1∈V1u_{1}\in V_{1} and u2∈V2u_{2}\in V_{2}. □\Box

We now turn to providing a positive certificate for strongly connected digraphs, based on the concept of ear decomposition [3, Section 5.3].

Definition 2.1 (Ear and ear decomposition)

Let G=(V,A)G=(V,A) be a digraph. An ear of GG is a directed path {(ui,ui+1)}i=1,…,k⊂A\{(u_{i},u_{i+1})\}_{i=1,\dots,k}\subset A such that for any i∈[[2,k]]i\in[\![2,k]\!], uiu_{i} is the head and the tail of exactly one arc in AA.

The graph GG possesses an ear decomposition if there exists a sequence of digraphs {Gi=(Vi,Ai)}i=1,…,s\{G_{i}=(V_{i},A_{i})\}_{i=1,\dots,s} such that

  1. (i)

    V1⊆V2⊆⋯⊆Vs=VV_{1}\subseteq V_{2}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq V_{s}=V,

  2. (ii)

    A1⊆A2⊆⋯⊆As=AA_{1}\subseteq A_{2}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq A_{s}=A,

  3. (iii)

    G1G_{1} consists of one vertex and no arcs,

  4. (iv)

    For any i∈[[2,s]]i\in[\![2,s]\!], Ai\Ai−1A_{i}\backslash A_{i-1} defines an ear of GiG_{i}.

Figure 1 below provides an example of a strongly connected graph that possesses an ear decomposition. In fact, ear decompositions characterize strongly connected digraphs in the following sense.

Theorem 2.1

[25, Theorem 6.9] A digraph GG is strongly edge-connected if and only if it possesses an ear decomposition.

Theorem 2.1 thus provides a positive certificate for the strongly connected property. In this paper, we aim at generalizing the result of Theorem 2.1 to positive spanning sets, which we define in the next section.

3 Positive spanning sets

The notion of positive spanning set (PSS) is a classical concept from linear algebra. The first part of this section reviews classical results on PSSs, while the second part draws connections between PSSs and strongly connected digraphs.

3.1 Definition and characterization

Positive spanning sets are commonly defined as families of vectors, akin to spanning sets. In this paper, we adopt the following, equivalent definition based on matrices.

Definition 3.1 (Positive span and positive spanning set)

Let 𝕃\mathbb{L} be a linear subspace of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and m≥1m\geq 1. The positive span of a matrix 𝐃∈ℝn×m\mathbf{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}, denoted by pspan⁡(𝐃)\pspan(\mathbf{D}), is the set

pspan(𝐃):={𝐃𝐱|𝐱∈ℝm,𝐱≥𝟎m}.\pspan(\mathbf{D}):=\{\mathbf{D}\mathbf{x}\,|\,\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{m},\mathbf{x}\geq\mathbf{0}_{m}\}.

A positive spanning set (PSS) of 𝕃\mathbb{L} is a matrix 𝐃\mathbf{D} such that pspan⁡(𝐃)=𝕃\pspan(\mathbf{D})=\mathbb{L}. When 𝕃=ℝn\mathbb{L}=\mathbb{R}^{n}, the matrix 𝐃\mathbf{D} will simply be called a positive spanning set.

Several characterizations of positive spanning sets have been proposed in the literature. Proposition 3.1 summarizes those that are relevant for this paper [13, 23].

Proposition 3.1

Let 𝐃∈ℝn×m\mathbf{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}. The following statements are equivalent.

  1. (i)

    𝐃\mathbf{D} is a PSS for some linear subspace 𝕃⊂ℝn\mathbb{L}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}.

  2. (ii)

    pspan⁡(𝐃)=span⁡(𝐃)\pspan(\mathbf{D})=\spann(\mathbf{D}).

  3. (iii)

    There exists a positive vector 𝐱∈ℝm\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} such that 𝐃𝐱=𝟎n\mathbf{D}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}_{n}.

When the matrix 𝐃\mathbf{D} has full rank, statement (iii) of Proposition 3.1 provides a certificate that 𝐃\mathbf{D} is a PSS of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. For future reference, we now present a certificate that a matrix does not positively span the entire space, which is a variant of Farkas’ lemma [8].

Proposition 3.2

[4, Theorem 2.3] A matrix 𝐃∈ℝn×m\mathbf{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} does not positively span ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} if and only if there exists a non-zero vector 𝐲∈ℝn\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} such that 𝐲⊤​𝐃≥𝟎m⊤\mathbf{y}^{\top}\mathbf{D}\geq\mathbf{0}_{m}^{\top}.

The positive spanning property is invariant to several operations on matrix columns, such as rescaling or permutation. In addition, if 𝐃\mathbf{D} is a PSS for a given ℓ\ell-dimensional space, then for any invertible matrix 𝐁\mathbf{B}, the matrix 𝐁−1​𝐃\mathbf{B}^{-1}\mathbf{D} is a PSS for another ℓ\ell-dimensional space. These invariance properties imply that we can reduce the study of positive spanning sets to equivalent classes defined as follows.

Definition 3.2 (Structural equivalence)

Let 𝐃\mathbf{D} and 𝐃′\mathbf{D}^{{}^{\prime}} be two matrices in ℝn×m\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}. The matrices 𝐃\mathbf{D} and 𝐃′\mathbf{D}^{{}^{\prime}} are structurally equivalent if there exists a non-singular matrix 𝐁∈ℝn×n\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, a permutation matrix 𝐏∈ℝm×m\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} and a diagonal matrix 𝚫∈ℝm×m\mathbf{\Delta}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} with positive diagonal entries such that

𝐃′=𝐁−1𝐃𝐏𝚫.\mathbf{D}^{{}^{\prime}}\;=\;\mathbf{B}^{-1}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{\Delta}.

We then write 𝐃≡𝐃′\mathbf{D}\equiv\mathbf{D}^{{}^{\prime}}.

Note that the notion of structural equivalence for PSSs was previously stated in the context of derivative-free optimization for families of vectors [5, Definition 2.3]. By adapting this definition to matrices, we can combine Definition 3.2 together with Proposition 3.1 to obtain a characterization of PSSs based on structural equivalence. This characterization involves matrices that have a particularly simple expression, thanks to the rescaling and permutation operators.

Proposition 3.3

A matrix 𝐃∈ℝn×m\mathbf{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} is a PSS of some ℓ\ell-dimensional subspace 𝕃\mathbb{L} of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} if and only if there exists m−nm-n vectors 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1},…\dots,𝐯m−n\mathbf{v}_{m-n} in ℝℓ\mathbb{R}^{\ell} such that

𝐃≡[𝐈ℓ𝐯1⋯𝐯m−n𝟎n−ℓ,ℓ𝟎n−ℓ⋯𝟎n−ℓ]and∑i=1m−n𝐯i=−𝟏ℓ.\mathbf{D}\;\equiv\;\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{I}_{\ell}&\mathbf{v}_{1}&\cdots&\mathbf{v}_{m-n}\\ \mathbf{0}_{n-\ell,\ell}&\mathbf{0}_{n-\ell}&\cdots&\mathbf{0}_{n-\ell}\end{bmatrix}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\sum_{i=1}^{m-n}\mathbf{v}_{i}=-\mathbf{1}_{\ell}. (1)

In particular, if m=ℓ+1m=\ell+1, one has

𝐃≡[𝐈ℓ−𝟏ℓ𝟎n−ℓ,ℓ𝟎n−ℓ].\mathbf{D}\;\equiv\;\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{I}_{\ell}&-\mathbf{1}_{\ell}\\ \mathbf{0}_{n-\ell,\ell}&\mathbf{0}_{n-\ell}\end{bmatrix}. (2)

The second part of Proposition 3.3 provides a characterization of a subclass of PSSs called minimal positive bases (see Section 5 for a formal definition). However, for general matrices, the structural equivalence (1) is not satisfactory, as it does not provide an easy certificate for verifying whether a matrix is a PSS of a given subspace.

3.2 Connection with digraphs

Having defined key concepts associated with PSSs, we now formalize their relationship with (strongly connected) digraphs. Although existing connections involve incidence matrices [19], our results rely more generally on network matrices [25].

Definition 3.3 (Network matrix)

Let G=(V,A)G=(V,A) be a digraph with A={(uj,vj)}j=1mA=\{(u_{j},v_{j})\}_{j=1}^{m} and let T=(V,A^)T=(V,\hat{A}) be an oriented spanning tree with A^={(u^i,v^i)}i=1n\hat{A}=\{(\hat{u}_{i},\hat{v}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}. The network matrix associated with GG and TT is the matrix 𝐌∈ℝn×m\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} defined by

∀i∈[[1,n]],∀j∈[[1,m]],𝐌i,j={0if the path uj−vj in T does not pass through (u^i,v^i),1if uj−vj passes through (u^i,v^i) in forward direction,−1if uj−vj passes through (u^i,v^i) in backward direction.\forall i\in[\![1,n]\!],\ \forall j\in[\![1,m]\!],\quad\mathbf{M}_{i,j}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}0&\text{if the path $u_{j}-v_{j}$ in $T$ does not pass through $(\hat{u}_{i},\hat{v}_{i})$,}\\ 1&\text{if $u_{j}-v_{j}$ passes through $(\hat{u}_{i},\hat{v}_{i})$ in forward direction,}\\ -1&\text{if $u_{j}-v_{j}$ passes through $(\hat{u}_{i},\hat{v}_{i})$ in backward direction.}\end{array}\right.

An example of network matrix is provided in Figure 2.

Several remarks are in order regarding Definition 3.3. First, note that there is no ambiguity in the definition as any path joining two vertices in TT is unique. Secondly, notice that we arbitrarily selected an ordering of the arcs in both AA and A^\hat{A}. Two network matrices defined using a different ordering of those arcs are structurally equivalent in the sense of Definition 3.2 [25, (36) p.277]. In the rest of the paper, unless otherwise needed, we will not specify the arc ordering. Finally, one may consider the incidence matrix of a digraph G=(V,A)G=(V,A) as a network matrix associated with GG and with the spanning tree T=(V∪{u},{(u,v)}v∈V)T=(V\cup\{u\},\{(u,v)\}_{v\in V}).

In this paper, for simplicity, we focus on network matrices whose associated spanning tree TT is a subgraph of the associated digraph GG, as such matrices are structurally equivalent to one another. For sake of completeness, we state and prove this property in the proposition below.

Proposition 3.4

Let G=(V,A)G=(V,A) be a strongly connected digraph with |V|=n+1|V|=n+1 and |A|=m|A|=m. Let T=(V,A^)T=(V,\hat{A}) with A^⊂A\hat{A}\subset A be a spanning tree of GG and let 𝐌∈ℝn×m\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} be the associated network matrix. Then, a matrix 𝐌′\mathbf{M}^{\prime} is a network matrix for GG and a spanning tree T′T^{\prime} if and only if 𝐌′=𝐁−1​𝐌𝐏\mathbf{M}^{\prime}=\mathbf{B}^{-1}\mathbf{MP} where 𝐁∈ℝn×n\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is nonsingular, col⁡(𝐁)⊂col⁡(𝐌)\cols(\mathbf{B})\subset\cols(\mathbf{M}) and 𝐏∈ℝm×m\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} is a permutation matrix.

Since 𝐌\mathbf{M} is a network matrix, we thus have 𝐜i=𝐞i\mathbf{c}_{i}=\mathbf{e}_{i} for every i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\dots,n\}, while any 𝐜i\mathbf{c}_{i} with i∈{m+1,…,n}i\in\{m+1,\dots,n\} has coefficients in {−1,0,1}\{-1,0,1\}.

Then, for any 1≤j≤n1\leq j\leq n, we have 𝐜ij′=𝐞j\mathbf{c}_{i_{j}}^{\prime}=\mathbf{e}_{j}.
